name: The Legal Ground
title: The Legal Ground
answer: Schools still have legal duties to English learners even though federal guidance was rescinded in 2025. The underlying civil rights law and court decisions remain in place, so schools must still provide meaningful access to grade level content. Districts should watch their state education agency for guidance and verify the status of federal changes before relying on any federal resource.

sections.body: This idea concerns the legal ground under English learner education, which rests on Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, the Supreme Court's decision in Lau v. Nichols, and the Castañeda v. Pickard standard. These authorities require schools to help students overcome language barriers. In 2015, the Departments of Education and Justice issued a letter explaining how schools could meet those duties, and in August 2025 the Department of Education rescinded it. The problem this idea solves is confusion: the rescission changed the guidance, not the law, so schools may wrongly believe their obligations have ended. The letter was not legally binding, and the statutes and court decisions it described remain in place.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, this means English learners must still receive meaningful access to grade level content, and Every Student Succeeds Act requirements for English learners still apply. Many states also have their own laws on English learner education, so local practice may go beyond federal requirements. The text does not give grade band examples, so the practical work is the same across ages: keep services in place and do not treat the rescinded letter as a reason to reduce them. Districts should watch their state education agency for guidance and check the status of these changes before relying on any federal resource. The federal office that oversees English learner programs is also in flux, since in April 2026 the Department of Education notified Congress that it planned to dissolve its Office of English Language Acquisition.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text labels this idea's evidence through news reporting rather than a study. It cites Education Week in 2025 for the rescission of the 2015 letter and for the point that the rescission changed guidance, not law, and that the letter was not legally binding. It cites Colorín Colorado in 2025 for the continuing Every Student Succeeds Act requirements and state laws. It cites Education Week in 2026 for the Department of Education's notification to Congress that it planned to dissolve its Office of English Language Acquisition. The text also notes that advocates say schools' federal duties to these students remain with or without the office.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are about what changed and what did not. The rescission removed guidance, not legal duties, so no one should read it as permission to cut services. The text warns districts to check the status of these changes before relying on any federal resource, because the federal office overseeing English learner programs is in flux. Decisions about how to meet the duties stay with schools and states, which should watch their state education agency for guidance. The text does not say who must make particular decisions, so it leaves those choices to local and state authorities.
